power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Behavioural models are used to forecast outcomes, interpret psychological processes and assess interventions.

We develop an account of model warrant centred on the claim being made: a defeasible justification tied to a specified inference, its target conditions and the assumptions connecting a model to behaviour.
Predictive, process and intervention warrants identify overlapping evidential obligations rather than a hierarchy or an exhaustive account of understanding.
The organising question is whether accounts compatible with the available observations disagree about the conclusion being drawn.
An analytical example shows that a binary logit curve can coincide exactly with the choice probabilities of a simple diffusion model, while leaving its temporal commitments untested.
We distinguish the additional constraints supplied by response times from the separate requirements of parameter identification, recovery and construct validation.
A second constructed example gives two accounts with identical observational choice distributions but different intervention effects.
These examples locate the extra assumptions or observations needed to extend a model's interpretation.
They also identify conclusions that remain defensible under uncertainty: predictive competence, partial process knowledge and decisions robust across specified alternatives.
We propose a concise statement of warrant that connects each substantive claim to its evidence, scope and unresolved alternatives.
This approach makes model evaluation more informative for psychological theory without reducing understanding to fit, transparency or an exhaustive description of mechanism.
A model fitted to choices may subsequently be used to describe preferences, explain a decision process, or appraise an intervention.

A coefficient first introduced to improve prediction can acquire the name of a psychological construct; a parameter that varies across experimental conditions can become a proposed target for changing behaviour.
These uses raise different questions about the same fitted object.
Accurate forecasts, defensible interpretations of latent processes, and credible estimates of intervention effects are all valuable achievements.
Assessing one does not settle the others.
The difficulty is to determine which conclusions survive a change in what the model is being asked to do.
This difficulty is familiar in several forms.
The distinction between explanation and prediction has consequences throughout statistical modelling, including variable selection and evaluation (Shmueli, 2010).
text.formatted: The distinction between explanation and prediction has consequences throughout statistical modelling, including variable selection and evaluation <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Shmueli, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Predictive assessment can improve psychological research by requiring models to succeed on observations beyond those used for estimation (Yarkoni & Westfall, 2017).
text.formatted: Predictive assessment can improve psychological research by requiring models to succeed on observations beyond those used for estimation <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Yarkoni & Westfall, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Formalisation makes theoretical commitments explicit, but those commitments still require an empirical connection to their target (Guest & Martin, 2021).
text.formatted: Formalisation makes theoretical commitments explicit, but those commitments still require an empirical connection to their target <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Guest & Martin, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Recent discussions of understanding sharpen the question of what a successful model establishes (Shiffrin et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Recent discussions of understanding sharpen the question of what a successful model establishes <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Shiffrin et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The problem therefore concerns the interpretation of success as much as the detection of failure.

Several contributions already address important parts of this problem. Motz et al. (2026) relate understanding to the purpose for which it is sought. Timokhov (2026) distinguishes interpretations of evidence accumulation models, while Bachmann et al. (2026) emphasise the difficulty of carrying laboratory accounts into practical settings.
text.formatted: Several contributions already address important parts of this problem. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Motz et al. (2026)</ref> relate understanding to the purpose for which it is sought. <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Timokhov (2026)</ref> distinguishes interpretations of evidence accumulation models, while <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bachmann et al. (2026)</ref> emphasise the difficulty of carrying laboratory accounts into practical settings.

text.text: Within theoretical psychology, Vanhasbroeck et al. (2026) argue that neither phenomena nor detailed data should serve as an exclusive basis for validating a theory. Almaatouq and Na (2026) develop ways of integrating explanation and prediction through experimental design, generalisation and interpretation.
text.formatted: Within theoretical psychology, <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Vanhasbroeck et al. (2026)</ref> argue that neither phenomena nor detailed data should serve as an exclusive basis for validating a theory. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Almaatouq and Na (2026)</ref> develop ways of integrating explanation and prediction through experimental design, generalisation and interpretation.

text.text: These arguments give good reasons to resist a single, undifferentiated standard of modelling success.
A related recent preprint by Chuang and Guest (2026) examines the justification of transitions across the computational modelling chain.
text.formatted: A related recent preprint by <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Chuang and Guest (2026)</ref> examines the justification of transitions across the computational modelling chain.

text.text: The need to justify transfers of empirical sup-port is therefore not itself a new claim.
Our focus is on the inference sought from a model in a particular domain: accounts can agree with the observations while disagreeing about a process, a construct or an intervention.
This focus complements scrutiny of the links between theoretical specification, implementation and empirical assessment.
Our contribution is to organise the evidential obligations associated with particular claims and to show how they change across uses of a behavioural model.
We distinguish predictive, process, and intervention warrants.
The term warrant refers here to a defeasible justification for accepting a specified claim, given the observations, modelling assumptions and target setting.
It does not name an intrinsic quality of an equation or a score that can be assigned to a model once and for all.
A model may be well supported for one purpose while an apparently small extension of its interpretation remains unsupported.
The organising question is whether accounts that remain compatible with the available observations disagree about the claim being made.
Such disagreement can be exposed analytically, even before new data are collected.
A familiar connection between binary logit and diffusion models illustrates how identical choice probabilities leave substantive process commitments unresolved.
A second constructed example shows how identical observational associations are compatible with different intervention effects.
Alongside these examples, we distinguish statistical identifiability, parameter recovery and construct validity.
The purpose is to make clear what additional evidence would change an assessment, rather than simply to counsel caution about models.
The argument applies across mathematical psychology, cognitive modelling and econometric choice analysis.
These fields provide different resources for specifying and testing behavioural accounts, and no exclusive association between a field and a warrant is assumed.
We also use intervention warrant more narrowly than policy justification.
An estimate of what an intervention would do is a scientific input to a decision; the decision additionally depends on whose outcomes matter, feasible alternatives and the consequences of error.
Keeping these questions visible allows useful modelling contributions to be recognised without asking a single successful analysis to establish more than it can.
A statement that a model has been validated is incomplete until the object of validation is specified.
It might refer to reproducing a distribution, estimating a parameter within a model family, representing a psychological operation, or forecasting a response to an action.
These claims can involve the same data and software, but their truth conditions differ.
A numerical routine may solve the intended equations correctly while the equations misrepresent the target behaviour.
Conversely, an idealised model may capture a useful dependence without describing every operation that produces an observed response.
We therefore assess a claim together with its scope.
Scope includes the population, task, outcome, measurement procedure and conditions to which the claim refers.
It also includes the resolution at which the claim is made.
A model may describe average choice shares adequately while failing to distinguish individuals; it may reproduce a response-time distribution while misrepresenting sequential dependence.
Agreement at one resolution is evidence about that resolution.
Treating it as validation of an entire account silently broadens the object being evaluated.
Warrant also depends on assumptions that connect formal quantities to observations.
These include the observation model, sampling conditions and restrictions on how parameters vary.
Calling a threshold response caution, for example, commits the modeller to more than an algebraic stopping rule.
It connects a mathematical feature to a psychological interpretation.
Calling a fare coefficient a causal response adds assumptions about why fares vary and what would remain stable if they were changed.
Such assumptions can be reasonable, but their status should remain distinguishable from facts established by the fit itself.
This use of warrant is deliberately modest.
It accommodates different inferential methods and permits support to be partial or revisable.
We do not offer a new probability calculus for theoretical claims.
Instead, we ask modellers to specify what an analysis justifies and where that justification relies on substantive commitments.
Evidence can strengthen a claim without uniquely proving it, and a claim may be useful before all plausible alternatives have been examined.
The appropriate conclusion then retains those qualifications.
Understanding is not exhausted by the possession of a warranted forecast.
A researcher may know that a forecasting system is reliable without grasping why a behavioural pattern occurs.
Philosophical accounts that emphasise intelligibility and the ability to work with a theory make the user's capacities relevant to understanding (de Regt & Dieks, 2005).
text.formatted: Philosophical accounts that emphasise intelligibility and the ability to work with a theory make the user's capacities relevant to understanding <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(de Regt & Dieks, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Work on idealisation also gives reasons to reject a requirement that an explanatory model reproduce its target in every detail (Potochnik, 2017).
text.formatted: Work on idealisation also gives reasons to reject a requirement that an explanatory model reproduce its target in every detail <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Potochnik, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: These positions caution against equating understanding either with prediction alone or with an exhaustive reconstruction of mechanism.
There is a further distinction between understanding a model and understanding through it.
An analyst can derive exactly how a diffusion threshold changes a response-time distribution.
This is knowledge of a mathematical system.
Applying the result to a person's caution requires evidence that the system captures the relevant aspects of that person's behaviour.
The derivation does not supply this connection merely by being exact.
Equally, an interpretable regression coefficient may be easy to explain while its connection to the target construct remains uncertain.
Opacity creates a different problem.

Difficulty inspecting a model's internal operations can obstruct particular inquiries, but it is not a general proof that the model cannot contribute to understanding. Sullivan (2022) distinguishes opacity from uncertainty about the connection between a model and its target.
text.formatted: Difficulty inspecting a model's internal operations can obstruct particular inquiries, but it is not a general proof that the model cannot contribute to understanding. <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Sullivan (2022)</ref> distinguishes opacity from uncertainty about the connection between a model and its target.

text.text: This distinction matters here: a transparent model can have an inadequately supported target interpretation, whereas a complex model can contribute to a well constrained account when the evidential connection is strong.
Transparency can assist scrutiny without substituting for that connection.
Accordingly, predictive, process and intervention warrants are not offered as three necessary and sufficient definitions of understanding.
They identify recurring claims made when behavioural models are credited with understanding.
Predictive warrant establishes a kind of competence within a specified domain.
Process warrant supports an account of how behaviour is organised or generated at a stated level.
Intervention warrant concerns the consequences of a specified change.
How these achievements contribute to understanding depends additionally on the question being answered and what the researcher can grasp or use.
The framework makes the evidential commitments of these attributions explicit.
The categories in Table 1 are neither exhaustive nor mutually exclusive.
text.formatted: The categories in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> are neither exhaustive nor mutually exclusive.

text.text: Models also support measurement, conceptual exploration, unification and demonstrations of possibility.
A simulation showing that a mechanism can generate a pattern may be valuable even before there is evidence that people use that mechanism.
It establishes a possibility claim under the simulated assumptions.
Its contribution should be assessed accordingly.
Measurement is especially important because it connects formal parameters to psychological constructs and can enter each of the three warrants.
Nor do the warrants form an obligatory sequence.
A randomised intervention can identify an average behavioural effect while leaving its cognitive pathway unresolved.
A process model can explain a qualitative pattern without providing the most accurate individual forecasts.
The same experiment can nevertheless bear on several claims: a manipulation may discriminate processes, test out-of-sample predictions and estimate an intervention effect.
What changes is the argument linking the observations to each conclusion.

Distinguishing warrants therefore supports integration of evidence, provided the connections are defended. an appropriate baseline and examining the distributional features relevant to the intended use makes the predictive claim more informative.
The value of predictive discipline lies in a specified test, not in the presence of the phrase cross-validation (Yarkoni & Westfall, 2017).
text.formatted: The value of predictive discipline lies in a specified test, not in the presence of the phrase cross-validation <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Yarkoni & Westfall, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: These issues are connected to the generalisability of psychological results.
A claim about a broad population of situations requires a design and analysis that address variation over those situations (Yarkoni, 2022).
text.formatted: A claim about a broad population of situations requires a design and analysis that address variation over those situations <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Yarkoni, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Precision obtained by repeatedly observing a narrow range of conditions cannot substitute for coverage of the domain to which the conclusion refers.
This applies equally to a flexible forecasting algorithm and a compact cognitive model.
For both, the validation domain is part of the claim, rather than a detail to be added after accuracy has been reported.
Prediction can be valuable without a process interpretation.
It can reveal stable regularities, identify where a theory's predictions fail, and provide a benchmark that a proposed explanation should meet.
The contrast between statistical modelling cultures drawn by Breiman (2001) helps expose the costs of evaluating models solely through familiar assumptions.
text.formatted: The contrast between statistical modelling cultures drawn by <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Breiman (2001)</ref> helps expose the costs of evaluating models solely through familiar assumptions.

text.text: However, pre-dictive success leaves a further question: which features of the target account for that success?
Correlated proxies, genuine causal dependences and compensating errors can each contribute.
The answer requires information beyond an undifferentiated accuracy score.
Process claims concern the organisation of behaviour at a specified level.
A sequential sampling model proposes a relation between evolving evidence, a stopping rule and a response.
A learning model proposes how experience changes a state that influences subsequent choices.
A process account need not specify neural implementation to be informative.
To favour one process account over a relevant rival, evidence must bear on a commitment on which they differ.
The mathematical detail of a model is useful insofar as it sharpens those commitments.

Goodness of fit becomes theoretically informative through this comparison. Roberts and Pashler (2000) show why agreement with data is insufficient when it is unclear which outcomes a model could accommodate.
text.formatted: Goodness of fit becomes theoretically informative through this comparison. <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Roberts and Pashler (2000)</ref> show why agreement with data is insufficient when it is unclear which outcomes a model could accommodate.

text.text: Work on model selection adds the importance of flexibility and the relation between fit and complexity (Pitt et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Work on model selection adds the importance of flexibility and the relation between fit and complexity <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Pitt et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: A more flexible model may fit because it captures a relevant process, because it absorbs omitted structure, or because it can reproduce a broad class of patterns.
A fit statistic alone does not distinguish these explanations.
Comparing serious alternatives and examining their qualitative commitments gives the numerical result a theoretical setting.
Joint observations can constrain an account more strongly than a single outcome.
In decision research, choice and response time connect a stopping process to both what is selected and when selection occurs (Forstmann et al., 2016; Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008).
text.formatted: In decision research, choice and response time connect a stopping process to both what is selected and when selection occurs <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Forstmann et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Additional measurements help when the competing accounts make different predictions for them and when the measurement model is credible.
More recorded variables do not automatically supply more diagnostic evidence: several measures may track the same ambiguity or introduce new interpretive assumptions.
The value of a measure lies in the distinctions it enables.
Successful prediction can consequently provide strong process evidence.
A prediction made before a diagnostic manipulation, and missed by plausible competitors, may be highly informative.
There is no general rule that prediction belongs only to predictive warrant.

Conversely, a failed prediction challenges a package of process assumptions, parameter restrictions and measurement choices; it does not uniquely identify the faulty component. Palminteri et al. (2017) emphasise the role of falsification and informative comparison in computational cognitive modelling.
text.formatted: Conversely, a failed prediction challenges a package of process assumptions, parameter restrictions and measurement choices; it does not uniquely identify the faulty component. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Palminteri et al. (2017)</ref> emphasise the role of falsification and informative comparison in computational cognitive modelling.

text.text: The practical objective is to design situations in which the proposed accounts have something consequential at stake.
The same choice curve Consider repeated choices between public transport and another travel alternative, conditional on a trip being made and both options being available.
Let Y = 1 denote choosing public transport.

Within random utility theory, this expression follows when the difference in random utility errors is logistic with an appropriately normalised scale (Train, 2009).
text.formatted: Within random utility theory, this expression follows when the difference in random utility errors is logistic with an appropriately normalised scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Train, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: The same choice equation can also be used simply as a statistical specification for conditional probabilities.
Its interpretation depends on the assumptions supplied with it.
By itself, Equation 1 contains no account of the time taken to decide.

Now consider a simple diffusion process with constant drift within each trial, where W t is standard Brownian motion, σ > 0 is the diffusion coefficient, and a decision occurs on first reaching one of the fixed boundaries -b and b, with b > 0.

It shows that even exact knowledge of the choice curve would not establish that choices were produced by accumulation to a boundary.
A sequential interpretation adds commitments that choice proportions alone have not tested.
This point is stronger than an ordinary comparison of two close fits.

A separate scale indeterminacy remains.
Multiplying b, v(x) and σ by the same positive constant merely changes the units of the evidence axis and preserves both choices and firstpassage times.
This is why an evidence-scale normalisation is needed.
It should not be confused with the previous transformation, which held σ fixed and changed the temporal predictions.
Stating the normalisation prevents a difference in arbitrary units from being interpreted as a difference in psychological evidence or caution.
Response times therefore enlarge the empirical target, but their force must be described accurately.
A logit equation that is silent about response time cannot be refuted by a time pattern it never purported to explain.
Rather, times distinguish specified process accounts and assess the extra commitments introduced by a diffusion interpretation.
Other process families may still accommodate the enlarged observations.
Support for the diffusion account is conditional on the competitors, constraints and measures examined, even if its parameters can be estimated precisely.
An experiment could make these commitments more informative by varying speed requirements or the quality of information while measuring choices and response times.
One candidate account might restrict a manipulation to the boundary; another might predict a change in drift or in the mapping between attributes and evidence.
Their jointly predicted patterns provide a basis for comparison.

Simply allowing every parameter to change in every condition, and interpreting the resulting estimates after fitting, weakens the connection between the experimental contrast and a particular process claim.
Parameter recovery asks a different question.
Data generated from known parameter values are fitted, and the resulting estimates are compared with the generating values.
This evaluates an estimation procedure under particular assumptions, sample sizes and designs.
Recovery can be poor even when parameters are identifiable in principle, because finite observations contain little information, parameters trade off approximately, or estimation is unreliable.
Good recovery establishes that the procedure can work in the examined generative setting.
It does not establish that human data were generated by that setting (Wilson & Collins, 2019).
text.formatted: It does not establish that human data were generated by that setting <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Wilson & Collins, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Model recovery likewise asks whether candidate generating models can be distinguished by the chosen comparison procedure.
It can expose a design in which one model is systematically selected even when another generated the data.
Its conclusions depend on which generators, parameter regions and observation processes were examined.
Neither a successful recovery exercise nor a more concentrated posterior distribution rules out misspecification outside that exercise.
These checks are useful resources for interpreting an analysis, but the claims they support remain conditional.
Hierarchical estimation adds another distinction.
Pooling information can improve estimation when participants have few observations, while the resulting estimates depend on assumptions about the population distribution.
A stable group mean need not imply that individual rankings are measured precisely.
If the substantive claim concerns individual differences, the uncertainty and stability of those differences must be examined at that level.
Precision in the grouplevel model cannot simply be inherited by every interpretation of its participant-level parameters.
Construct validity concerns whether a formal quantity can support an interpretation in terms of the psychological attribute of interest.
This requires engagement with the meaning of the construct and the relations in which it is expected to stand.

The nomological approach of Cronbach and Meehl (1955) and the account of validity developed by Borsboom et al. (2004) differ in their commitments, but both make clear that attaching a name to a score does not settle its validity.
text.formatted: The nomological approach of <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Cronbach and Meehl (1955)</ref> and the account of validity developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Borsboom et al. (2004)</ref> differ in their commitments, but both make clear that attaching a name to a score does not settle its validity.

text.text: Slaney and Racine (2013) further question how construct language is used and what it commits psychologists to.
A model parameter does not escape these issues by being inferred from a sophisticated likelihood.
A parameter labelled caution, for example, is defined in the model by its role in terminating accumulation.

Interpreting it as a person's stable tendency to deliberate requires additional claims about temporal stability, task dependence and the relation between the laboratory measure and the intended attribute.
An experimental effect on the parameter can support an interpretation, especially when predicted in advance, but it can also arise because another process changes in a way the model absorbs.
Parameter names provide hypotheses about this connection.
They do not independently test it.
Validation can combine theoretically targeted manipulations, independent measures and comparisons across specifications.
The contribution of each depends on its own assumptions.
Agreement between two measures that share a task artefact is weaker evidence than agreement across methods with different vulnerabilities.
A manipulation intended to change one construct may affect several operations.
A parameter's stability across model variants is useful only if those variants allow the relevant competing interpretations.
The question is whether evidence targets the proposed psychological meaning, rather than merely reproducing the same numerical regularity by another route.
Econometric choice modelling makes the scale issue especially visible.
In a random utility model, multiplying all utilities by the same positive constant preserves the choices.
For logit, the estimated coefficients combine systematic utility weights with the inverse scale of unobserved utility differences (Train, 2009).
text.formatted: For logit, the estimated coefficients combine systematic utility weights with the inverse scale of unobserved utility differences <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Train, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: A cost coefficient of larger magnitude in one population can therefore reflect a change in sensitivity, a change in unobserved variation, or both.
Flexible representations of heterogeneity do not automatically resolve this ambiguity; Hess and Train (2017) examine the relation between taste heterogeneity, correlation and scale.
text.formatted: Flexible representations of heterogeneity do not automatically resolve this ambiguity; <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Hess and Train (2017)</ref> examine the relation between taste heterogeneity, correlation and scale.

text.text: Ratios can remove a common multiplicative scale, but this achievement also has a limited scope.
Suppose deterministic utility is linear in cost and travel time and both coefficients are negative.
The ratio β t /β c is then positive and gives the marginal willingness to pay for a unit reduction in travel time under the maintained utility interpretation.
With cost in pounds and time in minutes, its units are pounds per minute.
Interpreting this ratio as a welfare-relevant value requires assumptions about preferences, the monetary attribute, functional form and the counterfactual being evaluated.
Scale cancellation does not establish those assumptions.
The same observed ratio has another reading in the diffusion construction.
With a common boundary and diffusion scale, the coefficients in the logit choice curve are proportional to the corresponding drift coefficients.
Their ratio then describes a trade-off in the specified mapping from attributes to drift.
The algebra does not decide whether that mapping measures subjective utility, attentional weighting or some other process.
A statistically identified ratio can consequently remain psychologically underdetermined.
This is precisely where identification within a model and validation of the model's interpretation must be kept distinct.
Intervention warrant concerns what would happen if a specified action were taken.
Examples include changing a fare, altering an information display or modifying the incentives of a decision task.
The target differs from predicting the behaviour of people who happen to face those conditions.
An observed association can depend on the process that allocated people to conditions, whereas the proposed action changes that allocation.
Causal accounts therefore require explicit assumptions about the relation between observed variation and intervention (Hernán & Robins, 2020).
text.formatted: Causal accounts therefore require explicit assumptions about the relation between observed variation and intervention <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Hernán & Robins, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This requirement is compatible with interventionist accounts of explanation, which relate causal claims to dependences that support answers to questions about changes (Woodward, 2003).
text.formatted: This requirement is compatible with interventionist accounts of explanation, which relate causal claims to dependences that support answers to questions about changes <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Woodward, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: It also explains why intervention warrant overlaps with some process claims without requiring a complete process account.
A well designed experiment can estimate an average effect while leaving the cognitive pathway uncertain.
Conversely, a plausible account of attention or accumulation need not specify all the circumstances that determine how a practical intervention changes behaviour.
It is useful to distinguish the intervention effect from the decision based on it.
For a bin- In the first account, receipt is random with probability 1/2.
Let E be an independent uniform random variable on [0, 1], and define Y = 1 when E < 1/4 + A/2.
text.formatted: Let E be an independent uniform random variable on [0, 1], and define Y = 1 when E < 1/4 + A/2.

text.text: Providing the concession changes the probability of public transport choice from 1/4 to 3/4.
The average causal effect is therefore 1/2.
Here the observed association reflects an effect of the intervention itself.

In the second account, an unobserved binary variable U is equally likely to be zero or one and determines choice, Y = U. It could represent a pre-existing disposition together with circumstances that make public transport feasible.
Concessions are allocated with probability 3/4 when U = 1 and 1/4 when U = 0.
This allocation produces exactly the same observed joint distribution of receipt and choice as the first account.
Yet setting A to either value leaves U, and therefore Y , unchanged.
The probability of public transport choice under either intervention is 1/2, so the average causal effect is zero.
Table 2 summarises the contrast.
Every observed combination of A and Y has positive probability, and concession receipt is possible in both latent groups.
The ambiguity is therefore not an artefact of an empty observed cell.
Unlimited observations of receipt and choice under the original allocation process would still leave the accounts observationally equivalent.
Predictive scores based on these shared observational probabilities are identical for the two accounts.
Crossvalidation using only receipt and choice therefore cannot resolve the causal disagreement: the accounts agree on the target that this validation exercise measures.
Note.
All quantities are analytically constructed, not estimated.
The do operator denotes setting concession receipt externally.
The average causal effect is the difference between the two intervention probabilities; 1/2 is a 50-percentage-point difference.
The text specifies each datagenerating account.
Additional outcomes distinguish these causal accounts only when they constrain the causal ambiguity.
Attaching the same conditional response-time distribution P(R | A,Y ) to both accounts would preserve their equivalence for the expanded joint observations (A,Y, R).
This construction does not claim that the accounts have independently validated, identical cognitive mechanisms.
It shows why merely collecting more behavioural measures cannot replace assumptions connecting those measures to the assignment and response processes.

Randomising concession receipt, or obtaining sufficient covariate information together with justified causal assumptions, changes the evidential problem in a way that extra repetitions of the same observations do not.
An effect identified in one study can still require further support before it is applied elsewhere.
Transportability concerns the conditions under which causal information from one population or environment informs another.
Such reasoning requires assumptions about relevant similarities and differences; it is not warranted by the size of the original sample alone (Pearl & Bareinboim, 2014).
text.formatted: Such reasoning requires assumptions about relevant similarities and differences; it is not warranted by the size of the original sample alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Pearl & Bareinboim, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The earlier predictive question about a domain reappears here, but the object being transported is an intervention consequence rather than only an observational probability.
In the travel example, a concession tested among existing public transport users might be applied to people with different access to services.
A short experiment might precede adaptation in departure times or residential choices.
If a large programme changes congestion, crowding or service frequency, outcomes for one traveller can depend on the responses of others.
An individual choice equation estimated under a fixed environment then supplies only one component of a system-level forecast.
The relevant time horizon, implementation and interactions belong in the target description.
Structural choice models are designed to address counterfactual questions by specifying how attributes, constraints and behaviour relate (Hess & Daly, 2024; McFadden, 2001; Train, 2009).
text.formatted: Structural choice models are designed to address counterfactual questions by specifying how attributes, constraints and behaviour relate <ref type="bibr">(Hess & Daly, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">McFadden, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Train, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Their value lies partly in making extrapolation assumptions available for inspection.
Those assumptions still need a substantive defence.
In the diffusion example, changing a fare attribute in a fitted drift equation assumes that the mapping from fare to evidence remains appro-priate under the proposed intervention.
A change in framing, attention or the feasible choice set can challenge that mapping even when the original response-time fit is good.
Intervention warrant can therefore be strengthened by evidence from the relevant perturbation, comparison across settings and sensitivity analysis over disputed assumptions.
When interventions cannot be observed directly, the conclusion should distinguish effects supported across plausible specifications from those that depend on a particular extrapolation.
Evidence of stability in some environments supports those environments; it does not establish unrestricted invariance.
This is a substantive limitation to report, not a reason to abandon counterfactual modelling.
What survives uncertainty about a model
The examples demonstrate limits on particular inferences, but they also identify conclusions that survive those limits.
Observationally equivalent accounts assign the same distribution to specified observables.
Where predictive adequacy has been established for a target draw under those conditions, unresolved process interpretations need not prevent a warranted forecast.
Requiring a unique psychological interpretation before using such a forecast would impose an evidential demand unrelated to that predictive purpose.
The scope of the justified claim determines which uncertainties matter.
The same reasoning applies within process modelling.
Accounts may disagree about peripheral components while sharing a supported claim about a particular operation.
A parameter combination may be identifiable even when its individual components are not.
Conversely, precise identification of every parameter within a restricted family can coexist with uncertainty about that family's psychological interpretation.
It is therefore useful to ask what aspects of a process are constrained, at what level, and relative to which alternatives.
Treating a model as either understood or not understood suppresses these distinctions.
This assessment does not require a catalogue of every possible model.
The space of pos- sible accounts is open-ended, and the importance of an alternative depends on the claim under examination.
In the choice example, a change in evidence units is irrelevant to behaviour, whereas a change that preserves choices but alters times matters to a temporal process claim.
In the concession example, allocation based on a latent predisposition matters to the intervention claim.
An informative comparison explains why its alternatives are serious possibilities and what conclusions they would change.
It also acknowledges where unexamined alternatives remain plausible.
Observational equivalence also does not imply equal credibility.
Independent knowledge of how a concession was allocated could rule out one of the constructed accounts.
Evidence from another task might favour a process restriction that the present choices cannot identify.
Such information belongs in the justification for the claim, with its own scope and uncertainty made explicit.
The point of the equivalence argument is to locate what the specified observations cannot settle, not to erase knowledge obtained elsewhere.
In a Bayesian analysis, for example, equal likelihoods for those observations leave relative support dependent on prior information; they do not require equal posterior probabilities.
Restrictions can resolve an ambiguity when they are independently defensible.
When they are merely convenient, the resulting conclusion remains conditional on that convenience.
Reporting their role prevents substantive assumptions from being mistaken for information extracted from the fitted data.
Exact equivalence is a particularly clear demonstration of insufficiency.
Empirical work more often encounters approximate agreement under finite data.
There, uncertainty about fit and uncertainty about interpretation must be considered together.
Two models can have similar overall performance while differing in a feature central to the intended claim.
A small discrepancy in the relevant tail of a distribution may matter more than a larger discrepancy elsewhere.
The substantive target determines which differences merit scrutiny; a single ranking of models need not serve every use.
One objection is that the framework privileges causal mechanisms by separating process from prediction.
This would be a problem if process warrant were intended to encompass all explanation.
It is not.
Philosophical work on distinctively mathematical explanation provides an explicit challenge to reducing explanation to causal process descriptions (Lange, 2013).
text.formatted: Philosophical work on distinctively mathematical explanation provides an explicit challenge to reducing explanation to causal process descriptions <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Lange, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: An account may explain through constraints, structure or relations that do not reconstruct a temporal mechanism.
Such explanations require their own connection to the psychological target, rather than automatic assignment to one of the present categories.
Our examples illustrate why this qualification matters.
Showing that a choice function leaves a boundary and drift trade-off unresolved is an informative mathematical result about the limits of an inference.
It helps explain why a particular design cannot answer a particular question.
It is not a proposed account of how travellers decide.
The result remains useful precisely because its explanatory target is clear.
The framework permits this contribution while retaining a distinct category for claims about the generation of behaviour.
Idealisation raises a related objection.
Since all models omit features of their targets, demanding extra evidence for every transition might seem to make understanding unattainable.
The relevant question, however, concerns the consequences of an omission for the claim at issue.
An idealisation can isolate a dependence and make it intelligible (Potochnik, 2017).
text.formatted: An idealisation can isolate a dependence and make it intelligible <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Potochnik, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: It becomes problematic when a conclusion relies on features the idealisation removes.
A fixed environment may be adequate for a local process comparison and inadequate for a forecast in which the proposed intervention changes that environment.
The standard is sensitivity of the inference to the omission, rather than completeness of description.
Uncertainty about precise consequences need not make every decision indeterminate.
If the remaining plausible models favour the same action under a stated objective and the relevant constraints, some unresolved differences may be immaterial to that decision.
This establishes a conditional robustness claim about the action.
It does not establish that the models share a mechanism, estimate the same effect, or exhaust every plausible account.
A sound recommendation makes clear both the agreement and the assumptions under which it holds.
The opposite can also occur.
Models may forecast baseline behaviour equally well but imply different preferred actions because they disagree about intervention effects or important distributional consequences.
The concession example supplies a simple instance: a costly programme could appear worthwhile under one account and ineffective under the other.
Averaging their predictions does not remove the underlying identification problem; it adds a choice about how to weight the accounts.
Sensitivity to that choice should remain visible to the decisionmaker.
This distinction helps direct further research.
An uncertainty that cannot change the proposed action may have little immediate decision value, although it remains scientifically inter- esting.
An uncertainty about who benefits or whether an effect survives implementation may be decisive.
The appropriate next study can therefore differ from the study that most improves average predictive accuracy or most refines an internal parameter.
Relating the analysis to its intended use allows those priorities to be argued explicitly.
The practical proposal is to attach a short, substantive statement of warrant to a modelling analysis.
The statement identifies the claim, the target conditions, the evidence that bears on it, and the assumptions on which the interpretation depends.
It also identifies a consequential alternative that the evidence has excluded or has left open.
This is not a demand for a universal numerical score.
Different studies can make different contributions, provided readers can determine what was evaluated and how far the conclusion extends.

For the choice example, a predictive statement would specify which participants or conditions were held out, what information was available for prediction, and which features of the choices were successfully forecast.
A process statement would add the temporal predictions and experimental contrasts that distinguished the accumulation account from named alternatives.
An intervention statement would specify how the effect of changing a fare was identified and why it was expected to apply in the target setting.
These descriptions make different evidential commitments even when they refer to parts of one research programme.
The strongest statements also describe a boundary that would matter in practice.
A result might depend on a fixed choice set, an observation window, an assumption about nondecision time, or the absence of interference between participants.
A meaningful limitation explains what inference would become uncertain if that condition changed.
General acknowledgements that models are simplifications provide less guidance.
Stating a specific boundary allows subsequent work to test it, relax it or deliberately restrict the application.
Reporting uncertainty at the appropriate level is equally important.
A narrow interval around a fitted coefficient describes uncertainty under the fitted specification and inferential procedure.
It need not include uncertainty about construct interpretation, omitted mechanisms or transport to another setting.
These sources of uncertainty may call for comparison across models, sensitivity analysis or further conceptual work.
They should not be compressed into the numerical precision of a parameter estimate merely because that precision is easy to report.
Once the desired claim is explicit, model checking and data collection can be directed towards the ambiguity that obstructs it.
If candidate accounts differ mainly in predicted decision time, collecting further choices alone may be inefficient.
If they differ in the assignment mechanism, an observational sample with more precise choice probabilities may leave the causal contrast untouched.
If the unresolved issue is the meaning of a construct, another recovery study under the same interpretation may be insufficient.
The additional evidence should bear on the particular disagreement, rather than simply increase the volume of observations.
Conceptual clarification is consequently part of empirical design.
A construct must be defined well enough for a manipulation or measurement to bear on it.
A theoretical claim must be specified well enough for competing outcomes to have different implications.

Eronen and Bringmann (2021) emphasise difficulties in building psychological theory that include establishing robust phenomena and relating them to constructs and causes. Scheel et al. (2021) similarly argue for work that develops concepts and phenomena before premature hypothesis testing.
text.formatted: Eronen and Bringmann (2021) emphasise difficulties in building psychological theory that include establishing robust phenomena and relating them to constructs and causes. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Scheel et al. (2021)</ref> similarly argue for work that develops concepts and phenomena before premature hypothesis testing.

text.text: These arguments complement formalisation: precision in equations is most useful when the empirical and conceptual questions to which they answer are also precise.
The framework leaves room for exploration.
Discovering a regularity, proposing an interpretation and revising a model after inspecting data are legitimate parts of theory development.
The evidential claim should record that sequence.
Agreement obtained by adapting a prediction to a known outcome cannot also be treated as an independent test of that prediction.
An exploratory parameter interpretation can motivate a study without being presented as an already validated measure.
This distinction protects the value of exploratory work by describing what it has actually contributed.
For theoretical psychology, the broader implication is that discussion of modelling success can become more exact without being reduced to a single statistical criterion.
The unit of evaluation is a claim made with a model under stated conditions.
This permits researchers working with different mathematical representations to compare the questions they answer, the observations that constrain them and the assumptions they require.
Disagreement can then concern a particular inferential step that is open to analysis or experiment.
A behavioural model can contribute to understanding by establishing regularities, constraining an account of a process, or supporting reasoning about a change in conditions.
The contribution depends on the claim being made and on the connection between the model and its target.
Predictive, process and intervention warrants identify several common forms of that connection without supplying an exhaustive theory of understanding.
The analytical examples make the distinction consequential.
A logit choice curve can coincide exactly with the choices generated by a simple diffusion model while leaving temporal commitments untested.
Two data-generating accounts can produce the same observed association between a concession and travel choice while implying different intervention effects.
Parameter estimation introduces a further interpretive step: identifiability and successful recovery within a specification do not validate the psychological construct attached to an estimate.
These limitations coexist with useful positive conclusions.

A useful analysis makes such possibilities visible and assesses whether the intended distinction survives plausible alternatives.

text.text: The contribution of the example is thus a concrete evidential progression: choices estimate a probability curve; additional observations test temporal commitments; targeted perturbations examine how those commitments change.

None of these steps licenses an unrestricted claim about the entire decision system.Parameters and psychological constructs Identifiability and recoveryThe diffusion example also exposes a difficulty with parameter language.
A quantity can have a precise mathematical role without having a uniquely supported psychological interpretation.
Statistical identifiability concerns whether different parameter values imply different distributions of the observables within a specified model and design.
If two values imply the same distribution, unlimited observations from that design cannot distinguish them.
The fixed-noise transforma-tion in the example creates such an ambiguity when choices are the only outcome.
Adding times changes the identification problem because it changes what is observed.

Other questions concern distributions, effects for subgroups or outcomes at a different time horizon.
None is automatically equivalent to recommending the intervention.
Recommendation requires objectives, costs, constraints and an assessment of how uncertainty affects the decision.
